size.note: Shoulder height (30–40 cm), head-and-body length (46–66 cm), tail (23–34 cm) and mass (3–5.3 kg) are given in both Wikipedia and Animal Diversity Web. Ear length is 11–13 cm on Wikipedia and 114–135 mm (11.4–13.5 cm) on Animal Diversity Web. Females are generally a little larger than males; that is not entered as a separate range.

summary: A small, greyish fox with enormous ears, a short muzzle and a bushy, dark-tipped tail, specialised for eating insects, especially harvester termites. It is on the Kruger checklist, but no recent Kruger records were found in this session.
description: The bat-eared fox is a lightly built fox with ears about 11–13 cm long, a short, sharp muzzle and a grey to buff coat. The legs are dark, the tail is bushy and usually dark towards the tip, and the face has dark markings. Sexes are similar in colour, and females are generally a little larger than males. Southern African animals belong to the subspecies Otocyon megalotis megalotis.
habits: In southern Africa it usually lives in monogamous pairs. In South Africa it is typically nocturnal in summer and more often active by day in winter. It forages mainly for insects, using its hearing to find prey in the soil and dung. It has relatively few vocalisations, with contact and warning calls heard most often in winter.

diet.summary: An insectivore, with a strong preference for harvester termites, but also taking other insects and, at times, small vertebrates and fruit.

young: Pups emerge from the den at about 17 days, are weaned at about 15 weeks, and are fully grown at about five to six months. A Kruger-specific birth-month range was not found.
habitat: Open short-grass country and lightly wooded savanna, typically with termites. In South Africa it is best known from arid parks such as Kgalagadi; a Kruger-specific habitat account was not found.

similar.note: The black-backed jackal is larger, with a silver-and-black saddle and smaller ears, and lacks the bat-eared fox's huge ear size and short muzzle.

population.notes: No Kruger population figure was found. The EWT 2025 assessment does not give a Kruger count, and no iNaturalist observations of any grade were found in Kruger (place 69020). The species is kept because it is on the 2011 checklist.
